title: The Applications of Large Language Models in Mental Health: Scoping Review
population: Adults and adolescents with or at risk of mental health conditions (depression, anxiety, PTSD, OCD, suicidality), social media users, patients in clinical settings, mental health professionals, and general public participants in vignette-based evaluations across multiple countries.
ai_type_application: Large Language Models (transformer-based, e.g., GPT-3/3.5/4, PaLM, LLaMA, BERT-derived models) applied to: screening/detection (depression, suicidality, anxiety, PTSD, OCD), clinical decision support and treatment/intervention assistance, counseling/chatbots, education/training content generation, and data augmentation.
mental_health_outcome: Primary outcomes reported across included studies include detection/classification accuracy and related metrics for depression, suicidality, anxiety, PTSD, OCD; quality of clinical decision support; performance on CBT-related tasks; counseling quality/summaries; intent to practice mindfulness/education engagement.
positive_effects: Across 95 studies, LLMs often matched or outperformed non-transformer models and sometimes human clinicians on specific tasks (e.g., OCD identification, crisis prediction, suicide risk screening); enabled efficient large-scale screening from social media and EHRs; supported clinical decision-making and CBT-related tasks; augmented scarce/imbalanced clinical data to improve diagnostic models; improved user intent to practice and experience in educational or supportive interactions; open-source mental-health–tuned LLMs available for targeted tasks.
negative_effects: Performance variability and hallucinations require human oversight; potential privacy risks and sensitive data leakage; training data biases may exacerbate disparities; insufficient reliability for direct-to-consumer health education without expert review; tendency to miss nuance (e.g., underestimate resilience) and inability to manage crises; risk of overreliance by youth and delayed professional care; limited evidence for complex clinical reasoning and empathy; heterogeneity of tasks and measures.
evidence_type: Scoping review of 95 peer-reviewed studies (2019–Aug 2024); narrative synthesis with comparative performance summaries and figures; no meta-analysis.
main_finding: LLMs show substantial promise for mental health screening, risk assessment, clinical support, counseling, and education—frequently surpassing prior NLP baselines and at times approaching or exceeding clinician performance on constrained tasks—yet require careful governance due to privacy, bias, safety, and reliability concerns; broader, higher-quality datasets and standardized evaluations are needed for safe clinical integration.
limitations_bias: No risk-of-bias assessment; heterogeneity of designs and outcomes precluded meta-analysis; exclusion of preprints; language restriction to English and Chinese; rapidly evolving models make comparative results time-sensitive; limited coverage of non-English applications and rare disorders.
relevance_to_our_review: High—summarizes effects of AI (LLMs) on mental health assessment, intervention support, and user-facing counseling/education, and highlights benefits and harms relevant to clinical adoption and public use.
notes_for_research_question: Use for background and to identify primary studies where LLMs improved detection (depression, suicidality, OCD), supported treatment decisions (bipolar depression), and influenced user engagement (education/mindfulness). Evidence suggests potential positive effects on screening accuracy and workflow efficiency, with notable safety and equity concerns requiring oversight.
